title: Iran and US Trade Compensation Demands as Hormuz Reopening Stalls; ADNOC Reveals 15 Vessels Hit; Senate Russia Sanctions Bill Targets India
subhead: Iran-Oman shipping lane talks reach final stages but Tehran insists on seven preconditions including US war reparations, while Trump counters with his own compensation demands. ADNOC says 15 of its vessels have been struck in Hormuz. The Senate-passed Graham Sanctions Act threatens 100% tariffs on Russian oil buyers, putting India directly in the crosshairs.

sections.heading: Hormuz Impasse: Compensation Demands on Both Sides
sections.body:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that an agreement with Oman on new shipping lanes through the Strait of Hormuz is in its 'final stages,' but reiterated that the waterway will not reopen until the US meets a set of conditions. Those conditions, outlined by Iran's national security secretary Mohammad Baqer Zolqadr, include US compensation for war damage, an end to military threats against Iran and its allies, removal of the US naval blockade in the Gulf, lifting sanctions, and releasing frozen Iranian assets.

Trump responded on Monday by demanding Iran pay compensation to the US for military deaths — citing roadside bomb casualties going back to the Iraq War and even the 2000 USS Cole bombing, which US intelligence attributes to al-Qaeda, not Tehran. The Wall Street Journal reported over the weekend that Trump has effectively abandoned his original war objective of securing a nuclear deal with Iran, now focused primarily on reopening Hormuz. Trump told Axios the US is 'low-keying it' and 'only semi-negotiating,' watching Iran's mounting inflation.

Oil prices rose on the impasse. Brent crude climbed above $88 per barrel on Tuesday, extending Monday's 5% surge, according to CNA and Reuters. IG market analyst Tony Sycamore called it a 'Mexican standoff' and projected oil would trade in the $75–95 range until one side blinks.
sections.whyItMatters: The mutual compensation demands have turned Hormuz negotiations into a credibility contest. Iran's conditions package is broad enough to serve as leverage for years, and Trump's counter-demands — including ones rooted in decades-old grievances — suggest neither side sees a quick resolution. The longer the strait stays closed, the more permanent the bypass infrastructure investments become.

sections.heading: ADNOC Under Siege: 15 Vessels Struck in Hormuz
sections.body:
Abu Dhabi's state oil company ADNOC said that 15 of its vessels have been hit by missile and drone attacks in the Strait of Hormuz since the conflict began, revealing a far wider toll than previously reported. The UAE condemned what it called an Iranian missile attack on an ADNOC-affiliated carrier transiting the strait on Saturday, calling it 'acts of piracy.' ADNOC said it is 'significantly impacted' by attacks on its people and assets, while still trying to meet customer commitments in an 'exceptionally challenging environment.'

The scale of damage to ADNOC's fleet underscores how even the Gulf state most determined to keep shipping through Hormuz is bearing heavy costs. ADNOC Gas separately reported a 52% profit drop in its latest quarter due to the Hormuz closure. The company still beat its Q2 guidance thanks to strong domestic demand cushioning the export blow, according to MSN.
sections.whyItMatters: Fifteen vessels hit is a staggering number for a single national oil company and reveals how systematically Iran has targeted UAE shipping. Despite paying Iran billions for safe passage (as Reuters reported in June), ADNOC vessels are still being struck. The financial hit — a 52% profit decline — shows that even wealthy Gulf producers cannot simply absorb Hormuz disruptions.

sections.heading: Houthis Hit Jazan Refinery After Makkah Pact Signing
sections.body:
Yemen's Houthis attacked Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery on Saturday, two days after Saudi Arabia signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement with Turkey and Pakistan. The Saudi energy ministry confirmed a fire broke out at the refinery but was extinguished with no injuries. According to Bloomberg and IIR Energy, Aramco has now delayed the Jazan restart to August 30, pushing it back two weeks from the previous schedule. The refinery had been shut since July 27 after an earlier Houthi strike.

The Houthi attack was framed as retaliation for the Makkah defence pact, which Saudi Arabia sees as a security guarantee against regional threats. Turkey's foreign minister Hakan Fidan said the pact was 'not directed against Iran or any other country,' but the Houthis clearly view it differently. They declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea last month.
sections.whyItMatters: The Houthis are now directly punishing Saudi Arabia for aligning with Turkey and Pakistan — expanding their targeting logic beyond Israel- and US-linked vessels to any regional actor making security arrangements they oppose. With Jazan offline for at least another three weeks, the refinery keeps illustrating how easily non-state actors can knock Gulf energy infrastructure offline.

sections.heading: ADNOC's $8B Gas Expansion and Hormuz Bypass Strategy
sections.body:
ADNOC announced on Monday an $8 billion investment to expand its gas business, including a new domestic gas processing unit at Habshan and a gas export facility at Ruwais. ADNOC Gas CFO Peter van Driel told Bloomberg the company is also weighing plans for an LNG export facility outside the Strait of Hormuz — in addition to the Ruwais LNG facility already under construction that will more than double export capacity to 15 million tonnes per year.

The UAE is building a second pipeline to Fujairah (outside Hormuz), doubling its export capacity by 2027. Meanwhile, Iraq and Syria signed a deal in July to rehabilitate a pipeline from northern Iraqi oil fields to Syria's Mediterranean coast — a project Middle East Eye first revealed has US backing. Rystad Energy's Artem Abramov told MEE that customers say they 'never want to deal with this again,' and that 'tens of billions of dollars' will be spent on bypass infrastructure.

The UAE also boosted oil production to an all-time high of 4.1 million bpd in June, according to the IEA, benefiting from its Fujairah pipeline that routes exports around Hormuz — and from having left Opec in May.
sections.whyItMatters: The financial logic of Hormuz bypass projects has shifted from prudent contingency to urgent necessity. Every Gulf state is now investing in alternatives, and the UAE — which already has the most developed bypass infrastructure — is using the crisis to expand market share after quitting Opec. The infrastructure being built now will reshape Gulf export routes permanently, reducing Hormuz's relevance regardless of when it reopens.

sections.heading: Graham Sanctions Bill: 100% Tariffs on Russian Oil Buyers
sections.body:
The US Senate passed the 'Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026' on August 7 with a full majority. The bill would allow the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% ad valorem on all goods from any country among the five largest importers of Russian crude oil and natural gas, or any country that continues purchasing Russian energy after the law takes effect. The identified targets are China, India, Slovakia, Hungary, and Azerbaijan. The bill also extends the Iran Sanctions Act through 2031 and targets reflagged oil tankers used by Moscow to evade existing sanctions.

India is the most exposed target. According to Kpler data cited by Fortune India, Russian crude imports to India surged from 1.09 million bpd in January to 2.78 million bpd in July, with Russia's share of Indian crude imports rising from 23% to 56% over the same period. The bill provides a waiver for countries sourcing less than 15% of their gas from Russia and taking steps to reduce, but India's dependence on Russian crude far exceeds that threshold.

India's government says it is taking a 'wait-and-watch' approach and believes the issue can be addressed through ongoing Bilateral Trade Agreement negotiations, according to a senior Commerce Ministry official. The bill now heads to the House, and Trump has indicated he would sign it.
sections.whyItMatters: The Graham Act would be the most aggressive US secondary sanctions regime on energy since the Iran sanctions of the 2010s. India's Russian crude imports have more than doubled since January, making it the bill's primary target. New Delhi's cautious response suggests it does not intend to cut Russian purchases voluntarily, setting up a potential confrontation where the US would have to choose between enforcing devastating tariffs on a major partner or granting exemptions that would gut the bill's credibility.

sections.heading: Pentagon's $400M Scandium Loan and the US Critical Minerals Push
sections.body:
The US Department of War's Office of Strategic Capital announced a conditional $400 million loan to Australian-listed Sunrise Energy Metals for its Syerston Scandium Project in New South Wales. The 25-year debt facility aims to establish the world's first primary scandium mine — currently, no primary mine-source scandium supply exists, and China controls roughly 80% of global mining production and nearly 100% of scandium processing. Sunrise chairman Robert Friedland called it a 'landmark moment' aligned with the US-Australia Partnership on critical minerals.

The Pentagon loan gives the US government a right of first offer on Sunrise's output, which would support defense industrial base companies. The announcement came alongside Trump's declaration that the US will invest $3 billion in critical minerals and battery projects to make America 'the minerals superpower of the world.'

Separately, India's federal government tabled the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill 2026 (MMDRA Bill) in the Lok Sabha, seeking to curb states' powers to regulate or tax mineral rights — a move Morgan Stanley called 'a key positive for miners,' according to NDTV Profit. The bill aims to centralize control over critical mineral resources, positioning India to better compete in the global minerals race.
sections.whyItMatters: The scandium loan signals that the US is moving from strategic mineral rhetoric to actual capital deployment — $400 million for a single mine is significant. But with China controlling 100% of scandium processing, the bottleneck isn't mining but midstream. India's MMDRA Bill, meanwhile, shows how critical mineral competition is reshaping domestic governance — central governments are stripping state-level authority over mineral resources to accelerate development.

bottomLine: The Hormuz standoff has become a mutual hostage situation: Iran demands war reparations and sanctions relief; Trump demands Iran pay the US for decades-old grievances. Neither side is blinking, and oil is climbing back toward $88 on the stalemate. ADNOC's revelation that 15 vessels have been hit shows the scale of Iran's maritime pressure campaign, while the UAE's $8 billion gas expansion and bypass pipeline investments signal Gulf states are building for a permanently disrupted Hormuz reality. In Washington, the Graham Sanctions Act threatens 100% tariffs on Russian oil buyers — with India's 2.78 million bpd of Russian crude imports squarely in the crosshairs. And the Pentagon's $400 million scandium loan to an Australian miner marks a shift from declarations to actual capital deployment in the critical minerals competition with China.
sources: Reuters, Middle East Eye, Kathmandu Post, CNA, Fortune India, New Indian Express, Moneycontrol, Economic Times, Oilprice.com, Bloomberg, Rigzone, MSN, The Hindu, NDTV Profit, IG Markets, Wall Street Journal, Axios, CSIS, The Diplomat
